gold_private.reference_answer: P is true for every real v; no unit-norm premise is needed. The output coordinates of vA are (bit,new bond). Expanding their squared mass gives ∑_{a,c} v_a v_c ∑_out A_{a,out}A_{c,out}. The inner sum is (AAᵀ)_{a,c}=δ_{a,c}, so the result is ∑_a v_a². In circuit notation U_{out,a}=A_{a,out} viewed in C, so U has 2r output rows and l input columns; U†U=I_l. For real inputs U times the column v equals the transpose/cast of vA because scalar multiplication commutes. A normalized output follows only when M(v)=1. The mass identity itself includes arbitrary norm and the empty-index cases.

stage_a_public.question: Let f be any real amplitude table on n+1 binary wires, with no positivity or normalization assumption. For an n-bit prefix b define m(f)(b)=sqrt(f(b,0)²+f(b,1)²), where (b,v) means appending last bit v. For any table g define N(g)=∑_w g(w)². Proposition P: N(m(f))=N(f) for all natural n and all such f. Decide P and explain the precise normalization invariant it supplies to a recursive loader.
stage_a_public.response_request: Decide whether proposition P holds as stated. Give the argument or an exact counterexample; diagnose the mathematical issue and state a valid repair when relevant.

gold_private.reference_answer: P is true for arbitrary signed and unnormalized real f. The radicand is nonnegative, so m(f)(b)²=f(b,0)²+f(b,1)². Sum over prefixes. Every (n+1)-bit word is uniquely (b,v) with v∈{0,1}, and reindexing along this bijection yields N(m(f))=N(f). Therefore N(f)=1 propagates to the marginal whenever it is actually assumed, and the equality also preserves any other squared norm. This is a nonlinear length-table reduction; it does not retain signed amplitudes or itself specify a linear quantum evolution. A recursive preparation circuit uses additional signed splitting data to reconstruct them.

rubric.criterion: Uses nonnegativity of the sum of two squares to square the square root.
Reindexes all full words by prefix and last bit, including both last-bit cases.

gold_private.reference_answer: P is false. Take f=(1,0), g=(-1,0). Then f+g=(0,0), so m(f+g)=0, but m(f)=m(g)=1 and m(f)+m(g)=2. All values are exact; each of the two inputs separately has squared norm one. Thus norm preservation does not imply additivity or a linear isometry. The marginal loses sign information (m(-f)=m(f)); it is a nonlinear preprocessing map on amplitude descriptions. The correct source claim is squared-norm equality for each table, not linear evolution under addition. Even restricting to normalized inputs would not define a linear subspace; unit-norm inputs in this witness already expose the inappropriate linear-map claim.
